title: Texas city demands $2M for public records on Flock usage
gist: As bipartisan backlash against Flock's AI license-plate cameras grows, Texas cities are quoting huge fees (up to $2.3M in North Richland Hills) for public records on usage, while a federal judge in Oklahoma called Flock 'indiscriminate mass surveillance' requiring a warrant, and few agencies opt into Flock's transparency portals.

insights.claim: North Richland Hills, a Fort Worth suburb, demanded $2.3 million to fulfill a records request for Flock data, claiming review of about a terabyte of communications would take roughly 14 years of labor at $15/hour.
insights.speaker: Ashley Belanger
insights.so_what: Prohibitive fees are emerging as a de facto barrier to accountability for AI surveillance deployments.
insights.quote: asked one group to pay $2.3 million before it would fulfill a public records request for Flock data
insights.locator: On Monday, the Texas Tribune reported

insights.claim: Fees for Flock records vary wildly by agency: across 200+ agencies queried, some provided 400,000+ pages free, others charged $5,000, and a Houston news station was quoted up to $121,000.
insights.speaker: Ashley Belanger
insights.so_what: Inconsistent transparency regimes make systematic oversight of ALPR networks nearly impossible.
insights.quote: Some cities provided more than 400,000 pages of documents for free, while others charged $5,000.

insights.claim: Texas DPS sought Attorney General permission to withhold the entirety of Flock data requested by the Texas Tribune, even after responding to an identical request covering earlier weeks.
insights.speaker: Ashley Belanger
insights.so_what: State agencies are hardening against disclosure as scrutiny rises.
insights.quote: the state Department of Public Safety has sought help from “the Attorney General’s Office to allow it to withhold the entirety” of Flock data
insights.locator: Additionally concerning are officials who deny

insights.claim: Very few agencies use Flock's optional transparency portals: of hundreds of Texas agencies using Flock, only 59 use portals and just 16 share data with the public.
insights.speaker: Ashley Belanger
insights.so_what: Vendor-supplied voluntary transparency tools are not producing meaningful disclosure.
insights.quote: In Texas, there are hundreds of agencies using Flock cameras, and only 59 agencies use transparency portals
insights.locator: However, very few agencies seem to be opting

insights.claim: Transparency demonstrably works: a USA Today records request exposed ex-Texas cop Zachary Anthony Klein's Flock abuse, leading to his arrest and guilty plea to 100 felony counts, and prompting Governor Greg Abbott to halt Flock funding and stop issuing permits.
insights.speaker: Ashley Belanger
insights.so_what: Disclosure-driven scandals can quickly cut off public funding for surveillance vendors, a material revenue risk for Flock in Texas.
insights.quote: Texas Governor Greg Abbott quickly halted Flock funding and stopped issuing permits
insights.locator: Texas is a perfect example of how

insights.claim: Many police officers have been found using Flock cameras to stalk strangers and people in their personal lives, and the article asserts Flock has yet to introduce meaningful reforms to address this.
insights.speaker: Ashley Belanger
insights.so_what: Unaddressed misuse sustains bipartisan backlash and regulatory risk for ALPR vendors.
insights.quote: Many cops have been found using the cameras to stalk strangers and people in their personal lives
insights.locator: The high price tags may be hiding data

insights.claim: Federal judge Sara Hill in Oklahoma ruled a Flock search unconstitutional, calling the network 'indiscriminate mass surveillance' that should require a warrant; the ruling sets no precedent but is among the first of its kind.
insights.speaker: Ashley Belanger
insights.so_what: A shift toward warrant requirements would sharply reduce the utility and value of ALPR networks to police customers.
insights.quote: That judge, Sara Hill, argued that Flock’s network “is a type of indiscriminate mass surveillance,”

insights.claim: Flock expects the Oklahoma ruling to be an outlier that will be appealed and overturned, while courts have so far largely held that police can access Flock databases without violating the Fourth Amendment.
insights.speaker: Ashley Belanger
insights.so_what: The legal status quo still favors Flock; watch appellate outcomes for regime change.
insights.quote: expects Hill’s ruling to be an outlier that will likely be appealed and overturned.

insights.claim: Audits reviewed by 404 Media show more than a hundred thousand warrantless searches of the Flock system every month.
insights.speaker: Ashley Belanger
insights.so_what: If warrants become required, this monthly search volume indicates the scale of usage at stake.
insights.quote: there are currently more than a hundred thousand warrantless searches of the Flock system every month.

insights.claim: Institute for Justice lawyer Michael Soyfer predicts Flock will use AI to let police set automated alerts for 'suspicious' travel patterns, citing federal agents using ALPRs to flag day trips across the border to justify stops.
insights.speaker: Ashley Belanger
insights.so_what: AI pattern-alerting would expand ALPR from lookup tool to predictive surveillance, raising both product value and legal/regulatory exposure.
insights.quote: I think Flock is going to automate that, using AI where cops can set alerts for those kinds of travel patterns.
insights.locator: We’re seeing that repeatedly with police

insights.claim: Advocates warn that new privacy risks will emerge as AI makes it easier to process data across the ever-broadening ALPR network, including access by hackers or bad actors to movement data.
insights.speaker: Ashley Belanger
insights.so_what: Data aggregation scale is the core risk vector; breach or misuse incidents could trigger regulation.
insights.quote: new privacy risks may emerge as AI makes it easier to process data across the ever-broadening network.
